question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(e), what must be true of trust account signatory authority regardless of how a Georgia real estate firm is organized (sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, or corporation)?
choice_a: Only a firm's outside CPA may hold signatory authority on trust accounts
choice_b: Signatory authority may be delegated entirely to an unlicensed office administrator
choice_c: Only the firm's registered agent for service of process may sign on trust accounts
choice_d: The qualifying broker must have signatory powers on all of the firm's trust accounts
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(e) requires the qualifying broker to have signatory powers on all of the firm's trust accounts, regardless of the entity structure the firm is organized under.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(e), does the statute impose different ownership/qualifying-broker structural requirements depending on whether a firm is a sole proprietorship, partnership, limited partnership, LLC, or corporation?
choice_a: Yes -- Section 43-40-18(e) specifies distinct ownership and qualifying-broker requirements tailored to each of those business-entity structures
choice_b: No -- Georgia law imposes exactly one uniform ownership structure on every firm type
choice_c: No -- entity structure is entirely unregulated and left to the firm's own bylaws with no statutory requirements at all
choice_d: Yes, but only for corporations; all other entity types are unregulated
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(e) sets out ownership and qualifying-broker requirements specific to each recognized entity structure -- sole proprietorships, general and limited partnerships, LLCs, and corporations -- rather than a single one-size-fits-all rule.

question: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(a) requires licensees operating from more than one place of business to comply with local business ordinances. Which Georgia statute does that subsection cross-reference for this local-ordinance obligation?
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(a) cross-references O.C.G.A. § 48-13-17 (part of Georgia's occupation-tax/local-ordinance framework) in establishing that licensees with multiple business locations must comply with applicable local ordinances at each one.

question: A broker's affiliated licensee posts a listing on a personal social media account, displaying only the licensee's name and personal phone number, with no mention of the firm. As a matter of Georgia's advertising rule (not a specific platform carve-out), how should this be evaluated?
choice_a: Georgia's advertising rule explicitly exempts all social media platforms from any firm-identification requirement
choice_b: Personal social media accounts are entirely outside any GREC licensee's regulatory reach
choice_c: Rule 520-1-.09's firm-name-and-phone-number and equal-or-greater-prominence requirements apply to real estate advertising generally, and are not confirmed to carve out social media posts from that obligation
choice_d: The rule applies only to yard signs and print media, confirmed to exclude any digital advertising
explanation: Rule 520-1-.09's core requirements -- that the firm's name and phone number appear, in equal or greater prominence than the individual licensee's -- are general advertising requirements; no confirmed platform-specific carve-out for social media was identified this session, so a listing post omitting the firm entirely raises the same compliance concern as any other advertisement.
source_note: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 520-1-.09(a)-(d); hedge: no social-media-specific carve-out confirmed

question: A licensee advertises a listing by stating the seller is guaranteed to net a specific resale profit if they buy through this same agent again within two years. What Georgia unfair-trade-practice concern does this advertisement raise?
choice_a: No concern -- guaranteeing a future resale profit is unregulated promotional language under Georgia license law
choice_b: It raises a concern only if the guarantee is later broken, not at the time it is advertised
choice_c: It is prohibited only if made in writing; an identical guarantee made verbally is unregulated
choice_d: Guaranteeing a resale profit is listed among the enumerated unfair trade practices under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b) enumerates guaranteeing a future resale profit as an unfair trade practice subject to GREC discipline -- the prohibition applies to the practice itself, not merely to instances where the guarantee is later broken, and is not limited to written guarantees.

question: A licensee places a 'For Sale' sign advertising a property for which the licensee has no listing agreement and no authorization from the owner at all -- essentially advertising the property speculatively. What does this violate?
choice_a: The enumerated unfair trade practice of offering property for sale, lease, or exchange without the authorization of the owner or the owner's authorized agent
choice_b: Nothing, so long as the sign is later removed within 10 days if no listing materializes
choice_c: Only a nonbinding GREC advisory guideline, not a statutory violation
choice_d: Only the sign-consent violation, not any separate offering-without-authority violation
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b) separately enumerates offering property for sale, lease, or exchange without the owner's (or the owner's authorized agent's) authorization as its own unfair trade practice -- distinct from, and broader than, the narrower sign-placement-without-consent violation.

question: A Georgia-licensed broker, without ever obtaining a license in another state, actively lists and negotiates the sale of property located in that other state. What Georgia license-law concern does this raise?
choice_a: No concern -- a Georgia broker's license automatically authorizes brokerage activity in every U.S. state
choice_b: Practicing real estate brokerage in another jurisdiction without being licensed there is enumerated as an unfair trade practice under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)
choice_c: It is a concern only for the other state's regulator, with no bearing on the broker's Georgia license
choice_d: It is permitted as long as the broker completes the transaction entirely by phone and email without traveling to the other state
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b) enumerates unlicensed practice of real estate brokerage in another state as an unfair trade practice under Georgia license law -- a Georgia license does not itself authorize brokerage activity in a state where the broker holds no license, and GREC may discipline the Georgia license for this conduct.

question: Georgia's real estate 'Firm' definition under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-1 is described as covering 'any business entity, including, but not limited to' several named examples. What does the phrase 'including, but not limited to' signal about the scope of that definition?
choice_a: Only the four listed entity types may ever qualify as a 'Firm,' with no other structure permitted
choice_b: The phrase has no legal significance and is purely stylistic
choice_c: The listed entity types (corporation, partnership, LLC, sole proprietorship) are illustrative examples, not an exhaustive/closed list -- other business entity forms may also qualify as a 'Firm'
choice_d: It means the definition applies exclusively to corporations, with the other terms listed as historical artifacts no longer in effect
explanation: The statutory phrase 'including, but not limited to' signals that the named entity types (corporation, partnership, LLC, sole proprietorship) are illustrative, non-exhaustive examples -- other business entity structures may also qualify as a 'Firm' under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-1's broad definition.

question: A firm's qualifying broker resigns, and the firm has not yet designated a replacement qualifying broker. As a matter of GREC rule (not a specific statute governing firm licensure itself), what is generally understood about a firm's ability to continue brokerage activity without any qualifying broker in place?
choice_a: A firm may operate indefinitely with no qualifying broker at all, with no time limit
choice_b: The firm must immediately and permanently surrender its license the same day the qualifying broker resigns, with no grace period whatsoever
choice_c: Only firms organized as sole proprietorships face any consequence from a qualifying broker's resignation
choice_d: A firm generally cannot continue brokerage activity indefinitely without a qualifying broker in place -- GREC rule affords only a limited window (commonly cited as around 60 days) to name a replacement before the firm must cease brokerage activity
explanation: Under Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 520-1-.07, a firm generally has a limited window -- commonly cited as around 60 days -- to replace a departed qualifying broker before the firm must cease brokerage activity, since a firm cannot lawfully operate as a brokerage indefinitely with no qualifying broker responsible for it.

question: As a matter of general national real estate office-management practice (not a Georgia-specific statutory figure), what is a commonly cited best practice for a brokerage's written office policy manual?
choice_a: Documenting supervisory procedures, advertising-review practices, and recordkeeping protocols in a written policy manual distributed to affiliated licensees, to support consistent compliance and to help demonstrate reasonable supervisory procedures if ever challenged
choice_b: Office policy manuals are legally prohibited in every U.S. state as an unauthorized substitute for statutory rules
choice_c: A written office policy manual is required to be filed annually with GREC for review and approval
choice_d: Office policy manuals need only be updated once, at the firm's founding, and never revised again
explanation: As a matter of general national office-management practice rather than a specific Georgia-mandated filing, maintaining a written office policy manual covering supervisory, advertising-review, and recordkeeping practices is a widely recommended risk-management tool -- though no GREC pre-approval filing requirement for such a manual was confirmed this session.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate office-management practice; not a Georgia-specific filing requirement confirmed this session

question: A firm changes its registered trade name (the 'doing business as' name it advertises under) but continues operating under the same GREC firm license. What is the general expectation regarding GREC notification of a trade-name change?
choice_a: Trade names are entirely unregulated in Georgia real estate practice, with no registration expectation of any kind
choice_b: A firm using a trade name distinct from its legal name is generally expected to have that name properly registered with GREC, consistent with the firm-identification purpose behind the advertising rule's firm-name requirement -- though the precise notification procedure and timeline for a trade-name change specifically were not independently pinned down this session
choice_c: A trade-name change automatically voids the firm's GREC license, requiring a brand-new firm application
choice_d: Trade-name changes may only be made once every 10 years under Georgia license law
explanation: Consistent with Rule 520-1-.09's requirement that advertising identify the firm's (registered) name, a firm operating under a trade name distinct from its legal name is generally expected to have that name properly registered with GREC -- though this session did not independently confirm the specific procedural rule number or notification timeline governing a trade-name change.
source_note: hedge: consistent with Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 520-1-.09's firm-identification purpose; specific trade-name registration rule text not independently retrieved this session

question: A brokerage wants to advertise a group of its agents together as a 'team' under a team name distinct from the firm's own registered name. As a matter of Georgia's underlying advertising-rule purpose (not a confirmed dedicated 'team advertising' rule), what would remain true regardless of the team branding used?
choice_a: Team advertising is entirely exempt from Rule 520-1-.09's firm-identification requirements
choice_b: A team name automatically replaces the need to identify the sponsoring firm at all
choice_c: The firm's own registered name and a phone number reaching the firm would still need to appear in equal or greater size, prominence, and frequency than the team name or any individual team member's name, consistent with Rule 520-1-.09's general requirement
choice_d: Only the team leader's individual license number, and nothing else, is required to appear
explanation: While no confirmed dedicated 'team advertising' rule text was independently retrieved this session, Rule 520-1-.09's general requirement -- that the firm's registered name and phone number appear in equal or greater prominence than any individual licensee's -- would logically extend to a team name or team-branded advertising, since a team name does not substitute for the firm-identification purpose the rule serves.
source_note: hedge: general application of Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 520-1-.09's firm-identification requirement; no dedicated Georgia team-advertising rule confirmed this session

question: Rule 520-1-.09 requires that a firm's name and phone number appear with equal or greater 'frequency' compared to an individual licensee's, in addition to size and prominence. What does the 'frequency' element specifically address, distinct from mere size?
choice_a: The number of separate advertisements a firm is permitted to publish per calendar month
choice_b: How frequently GREC audits a firm's advertisements each year
choice_c: The frequency element was repealed and no longer appears in the current rule
choice_d: How OFTEN the firm's identifying information appears throughout an advertisement (e.g., across multiple pages, panels, or repeated mentions), not merely how large it is displayed on a single occurrence
explanation: The 'frequency' element of Rule 520-1-.09 addresses how often the firm's name and phone number appear throughout an advertisement -- distinct from the 'size' element (how large each individual appearance is) and the 'prominence' element (how visually emphasized it is) -- preventing a firm from technically satisfying size/prominence once while an individual licensee's name is repeated many more times throughout the same ad.
